items.name: Earth Hour
clues: Once a year, millions of people around the world do something very simple, for exactly sixty minutes.
It was started by the conservation charity with a panda as its logo.
It began in Sydney on 31 March 2007, and it is usually held on the last Saturday in March.
From half past eight to half past nine in the evening, local time, people switch off their lights.
Landmarks such as the Eiffel Tower and the Brandenburg Gate have gone dark for it.
Its name: our planet, plus sixty minutes.

items.name: Kyoto Protocol
clues: The first global deal with legally binding cuts in emissions, but only for rich, industrialised countries.
Governments negotiated it at a UN conference. The USA signed it but never ratified it.
It was agreed in December 1997, but it only came into force in 2005, after Russia ratified it.
Countries that had cut more than their target could sell the difference to countries that hadn’t.
Canada pulled out in 2011, saying it made little sense without the USA and China.
It’s named after Japan’s old imperial capital, a city famous for its temples.

items.name: Pfand
clues: You pay a little extra, and you get it back later, if you can be bothered.
Almost every German supermarket takes part, and so does everyone who has ever been to a party.
Since 2003, Germany has used it on many one-way plastic bottles and cans.
You feed your empties into a machine at the supermarket, and it prints a receipt you can spend at the till.
It’s 25 cents for a plastic bottle or a can, so some people collect the ones that others leave in parks.
A campaign asks people to leave empty bottles next to the bin, not in it: “Pfand gehört daneben”.

items.name: Montreal Protocol
clues: It’s often called the most successful environmental treaty ever, and it isn’t mainly about climate change.
In 2009 it became the first treaty in UN history to be ratified by every member country.
It was signed in 1987, two years after British scientists in Antarctica reported that something high in the sky was disappearing.
It phased out chemicals that used to be in fridges and spray cans.
UN scientists expect the hole over Antarctica to have closed by about 2066.
It saved the ozone layer, and it’s named after a Canadian city famous for bagels and its Formula 1 race.

items.name: An Inconvenient Truth
clues: It made a slideshow famous. Really.
It’s presented by a man who came within a few hundred votes of becoming US president.
It came out in 2006 and won an Academy Award for best documentary.
Its presenter tours the world giving a lecture with graphs and photos, and at one point rides a lift to show how high one line on a graph has climbed.
The next year, the presenter shared the Nobel Peace Prize with the UN’s climate panel.
Al Gore’s climate film. Its title says the facts are true, but awkward to hear.

items.name: Paris Agreement
clues: Instead of being told what to cut, every country sets its own target and promises to raise it every five years.
Almost every government in the world signed up, after years of failed talks.
It was agreed at a UN climate summit in December 2015, held at an old airfield just outside a European capital.
Countries aim to keep global warming “well below 2°C” and to try to stop it at 1.5°C.
The USA has walked out of it twice, both times under the same president.
It’s named after the city of the Eiffel Tower.
